title: How Bitcoin works
subtitle: Building digital money from a shared list

scenes.narration: What does it mean to own a bitcoin?
scenes.question: What does it mean to own a bitcoin?

scenes.title: Who paid whom
scenes.narration: Start with something simpler. A few friends pay for each other’s dinners, and they keep one shared list of who paid whom.

steps.say: Alice pays Bob twenty dollars, so she writes it down.
More lines go on the list as the month goes by.
At the end of the month they settle up. Whoever is down puts cash in a pot, and whoever is up takes cash out.
But anyone can add a line. What stops Bob from writing that Alice pays him a hundred dollars?

scenes.title: Sign with a secret, check in public
scenes.narration: The fix is a digital signature. Each person makes a pair of keys: a secret key they never share, and a public key everyone can see.

steps.action: signs the line with her secret key
steps.say: Alice runs her line and her secret key through a signing function. Out comes a signature, a string of five hundred and twelve bits.

steps.action: checks it with her public key
steps.say: Anyone can check that signature against the line and Alice’s public key. The answer is true.

steps.payload: Verify(changed line, same signature, public key) → false
steps.say: If Bob changes the line, the old signature no longer fits, and the check says false. Without Alice’s secret key, he cannot make a new one.

scenes.title: Real signatures, first 64 of 512 bits
scenes.narration: Here are real signatures made with one secret key. Watch what happens when the line changes.

steps.say: This is Alice’s signature for paying Bob a hundred dollars.
Change one character, a hundred to a hundred and one, and the signature looks completely different.
Put the old signature on a changed line, and the check fails.
But Bob can still copy the whole signed line, word for word. The copy checks out, so Alice would pay him twice.

steps.callout: every line gets a unique ID
steps.say: So every line gets a number of its own, and the signature covers that number too.
Now a copy carries a number that is already on the list, and everyone ignores it.

scenes.narration: Signatures stop fake lines, but not debt. Charlie could run up a huge bill and vanish. So add a rule: everyone starts with a hundred, and a line counts only if the list shows the payer has the money.

steps.say: Charlie pays Alice sixty. He can cover it, so the line counts, and he has forty left.
Charlie pays Bob forty. That leaves him with nothing.
Alice pays David twenty. She has plenty.
Then Charlie tries to pay David thirty. Read the list from the top, and he has nothing left, so everyone rejects that line.
Notice that nobody holds any dollars now. The money is just the list, so call it ledger dollars. Owning some means the history says you have them.

scenes.title: Everyone keeps a copy
scenes.narration: So far one website holds the list. But then you have to trust whoever runs it.

steps.say: So drop the website. Instead, everyone keeps their own copy of the list.
To pay Bob, Alice broadcasts her signed line to everyone, and each person adds it to their copy.
But messages take time to travel. At the same moment, David sends a line of his own, and Charlie and David get his line first.
Now the copies disagree about the order. With no one in charge, how does everyone agree on one history?

scenes.title: Any text in, 256 bits out
scenes.narration: The answer needs one more tool, a hash function called SHA-256. It takes any text, short or long, and gives back two hundred and fifty six bits, written here as sixty four hex digits.

steps.say: This is the hash of Hello, with a capital H.
Change just that one letter to lower case, and the whole result changes. Nothing about it is close to the first.
And there is no way back. To find text with a given hash, all you can do is guess, and the guesses would outlast the universe.

scenes.title: Hunting for 30 zeros
scenes.narration: Now a puzzle. Take a batch of lines, add a number called a nonce, and hash the lot. The goal is a hash that starts with thirty zero bits.
scenes.callout: SHA-256(lines + nonce) starts with 30 zero bits?

steps.say: With a nonce of zero, the hash starts with only 1 zero bit.
So try one, then two, then three. Each guess gives a hash that looks random.
Our computer kept going for a few minutes, and this number finally worked. Each bit halves the odds, so thirty zeros takes about two to the thirty guesses, around a billion.
Finding it is slow, but checking it is fast. Anyone can hash the lines with this nonce once and see the zeros.

scenes.narration: Lines are grouped into blocks. A block counts only if it solves the puzzle, and each block starts with the hash of the block before it. That links them into a chain.

steps.say: Block one’s hash starts with the zeros its nonce bought.
Block two writes that hash at its top. So does every block after, about the one before it.
Now say someone changes an old line in block one, ten to a hundred. Its hash changes completely, and no longer starts with zeros.
Block two still points at the old hash, so the link is broken, and everyone can see it.

steps.callout: redo the work for every later block
steps.say: To hide the change, the cheat must solve the puzzle again for block one, then for every block after it.

scenes.narration: People called miners collect the lines everyone broadcasts and race to solve the puzzle for the next block.

nodes.caption: first line: 10 LD to miner Maya

nodes.label: Block 4
nodes.caption: first line: 10 LD to miner Omar

steps.say: Maya solves it first. The first line of her block pays her ten ledger dollars out of thin air. That reward is the only way new money appears.
But Omar solved a different block four at nearly the same moment. Now there are two chains of the same length.
The next miner happens to build on Maya’s block. That chain is longer now, and the rule is simple: everyone follows the longest chain. Omar’s block is dropped, and its lines go back into the pool.

scenes.title: Chance a cheat with a tenth of the computing power catches up
scenes.narration: Here is the attack. Alice pays Bob in one block, while secretly building another chain where that payment never happened. If her chain gets longer, everyone switches to it, and her money comes back.

steps.say: But her one machine races everyone else’s together. Say she has a tenth of all the computing power.
If Bob waits for one block on top of his payment, her chance of ever catching up is about one in five.
Each extra block makes it much smaller. After six blocks it is about two in ten thousand. So Bob waits a few blocks before he trusts the payment.

scenes.title: The reward halves
scenes.narration: That is Bitcoin. The network adjusts the puzzle every two thousand and sixteen blocks, about two weeks, so a new block comes about every ten minutes.

steps.say: In two thousand and nine, each block paid its miner fifty bitcoin.
Every two hundred and ten thousand blocks, about four years, the reward halves. Twenty five, then twelve and a half, then six and a quarter.
Since twenty twenty four it is three point one two five. Add up every halving and the total stops just short of twenty one million bitcoin.

steps.callout: plus fees, for a spot in a full block
steps.say: Blocks also have a size limit, so people add a small fee to their line, and miners pick the lines that pay them best. As the reward shrinks, fees pay more of the miners’ bills.

scenes.title: One tool for each problem
scenes.narration: Each problem we hit along the way got one tool.

cells: Anyone can write a fake line
A signed line can be copied
A unique ID on every line
People spend money they do not have
Copies disagree, and no one is in charge
Proof of work, and the longest chain wins
Redoing the work is too expensive

steps.say: Signatures and IDs stop fake and copied lines.
The shared history decides who owns what.
And proof of work, with the longest chain, lets strangers agree on one history without anyone in charge.
